n1-quiz-apply-create.enunciado: The recepcao pod already exists: you applied recepcao.yaml. Now you add a label to the file and run kubectl create -f recepcao.yaml. What happens?
n1-quiz-apply-create.vidaReal: create is a request for a brand-new build: if the apartment already exists, the doorman sends it back. apply is the updated blueprint: the doorman compares and changes only the difference.
n1-quiz-apply-create.limite: apply isn’t magic: almost nothing in a pod’s spec can change after it’s created (you can swap the image, but you can’t add a container), and then it’s delete and create again.

alternativas.texto: The pod gets the new label.
alternativas.explicacao: That’s kubectl apply: it creates or updates. create only knows how to create.

alternativas.texto: A second recepcao pod is born, already with the label.
alternativas.explicacao: No: in the same namespace, two objects of the same kind can’t have the same name.

alternativas.texto: Error: the pod already exists (AlreadyExists), and nothing changes.
alternativas.explicacao: Right. To update from the file, use kubectl apply -f; if nothing changed, it answers unchanged.

alternativas.texto: The old pod is deleted and created again, with the label.
alternativas.explicacao: Neither create nor apply deletes the pod to recreate it. A new label is something apply changes on the pod itself.

n1-quiz-namespace-rede.titulo: Quiz: does the namespace lock the door?
n1-quiz-namespace-rede.enunciado: Can the sala-de-reuniao pod in financeiro talk, over the network, to the sala-de-reuniao in rh?
n1-quiz-namespace-rede.vidaReal: Two companies in the same condo: different signs on the door, but the hallway is the same.
n1-quiz-namespace-rede.limite: In the condo, each company locks its own door. In the cluster, without a NetworkPolicy, no door has a lock.

alternativas.texto: No: different namespaces have separate networks.
alternativas.explicacao: That’s the most common mistake. The namespace separates names (and, later on, badges and quotas), not the network.

alternativas.texto: Only if both pods have the same label.
alternativas.explicacao: Labels don’t open or close the network: they’re only for picking pods.

alternativas.texto: Yes: by default, every pod talks to every pod, in any namespace.
alternativas.explicacao: Right. To close the way, there are turnstiles (NetworkPolicy), in level 8.

n2-quiz-reforma.titulo: Quiz: what does a version change create?
n2-quiz-reforma.enunciado: The loja (store) Deployment, with 3 replicas, runs 1.0. You change the image to 1.1 and apply. What happens under the hood?
n2-quiz-reforma.vidaReal: The renovation in stages: the new floor is built next door, the residents move a few at a time, and the old floor stays empty, kept in case you need to go back.
n2-quiz-reforma.limite: An empty floor would cost rent; a ReplicaSet with 0 pods costs nothing, but only the last 10 are kept (revisionHistoryLimit).

alternativas.texto: The existing ReplicaSet swaps the pods’ image, one by one, without recreating them.
alternativas.explicacao: No: the Deployment doesn’t renovate the old ReplicaSet, it creates another one (with another hash in the name). And the pods are replaced, not renovated: new name, new IP.

alternativas.texto: The Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet, scales its pods up and the old one’s down, a few at a time. The old one stays, with 0 pods.
alternativas.explicacao: Right. The old, empty ReplicaSet is the previous revision: it’s what kubectl rollout undo goes back to.

alternativas.texto: The Deployment deletes the 3 pods and only then creates the 3 new ones.
alternativas.explicacao: That’s how the Recreate strategy works. The default is RollingUpdate: a few at a time, without closing the store.

alternativas.texto: Nothing: the pods only get the new image when they’re deleted.
alternativas.explicacao: That would happen with a ReplicaSet on its own. The Deployment notices the new template and starts the swap right away.

n2-quiz-scale-e-apply.enunciado: On Black Friday, you ran kubectl scale deploy/loja --replicas=5. Days later, someone applies the loja.yaml from the repository, which says replicas: 3. How many replicas does loja end up with?
n2-quiz-scale-e-apply.vidaReal: The temps were hired over the phone, but the contract on file still says 3: when someone sends the contract again, the 3 is what counts.
n2-quiz-scale-e-apply.limite: To change the number for good, change the file. And when the HPA (level 6) takes care of the replicas, it’s best not to write replicas in the YAML at all.

alternativas.explicacao: scale changed only the cluster, not the file. apply writes what the file declares.
apply doesn’t add anything up: it makes the field match the file.
Right: apply sets replicas back to what the file says. A change made from the terminal is lost on the next apply of the old file.

n2-quiz-undo.enunciado: kubectl rollout history deploy/loja shows revisions 1, 2 and 3. You run kubectl rollout undo deploy/loja --to-revision=1. What does the history look like afterward?
n2-quiz-undo.vidaReal: Nobody tears pages out of the renovation log: undoing a renovation means writing a new page that says “we went back to the opening-day design”.
n2-quiz-undo.limite: In a paper log, the old page is still there. Here the old number disappears, because the ReplicaSet is the same one and just gets a new number.

alternativas.texto: 1, 2 and 3, with 1 marked as current.
alternativas.explicacao: The history has no “current” marker: the current one is always the highest number.

alternativas.texto: Only 1: revisions 2 and 3 are deleted.
alternativas.explicacao: Nothing is deleted: 2 and 3 are still there, so you can go back to them too.

alternativas.texto: 2, 3 and 4: revision 1 became 4.
alternativas.explicacao: Right: going back is moving forward. Revision 1’s template (the same ReplicaSet) gets number 4, and 1 leaves the list.

n3-quiz-sorteio.enunciado: There are 3 pods behind the loja Service. A client opens 3 connections, one after another. How does the extension split them?
n3-quiz-sorteio.vidaReal: The extension’s switchboard draws a clerk at random for every call: there’s no queue and no turns.
n3-quiz-sorteio.limite: At a real switchboard, the call goes to whoever is free. The Service doesn’t know who’s busy: it just draws at random.

alternativas.texto: Round-robin: one connection to each pod, in order.
alternativas.explicacao: It’s what almost everyone imagines, but kube-proxy (in its default mode) doesn’t keep track of anyone’s turn.

alternativas.texto: Each connection goes to a randomly drawn pod: the same pod may handle all three.
alternativas.explicacao: Right: a random draw for every new connection. With many connections the load evens out; with few, it can be lopsided. And it’s per connection: a client that reuses its connection (keep-alive) always talks to the same pod.

alternativas.texto: They all go to the least busy pod.
alternativas.explicacao: The extension doesn’t measure load: it doesn’t know whether the clerk is busy.

alternativas.texto: They all go to the first pod, until it goes down.
alternativas.explicacao: No: the Service spreads connections across all ready pods.

n3-quiz-porta.titulo: Quiz: which port do you dial?
n3-quiz-porta.enunciado: The loja Service has port: 80 and targetPort: 8080. From inside another pod, which address reaches the store through the extension?
n3-quiz-porta.vidaReal: The extension is the switchboard’s 80; inside, the clerk sits in room 8080. Callers dial the extension, not the room number.
n3-quiz-porta.limite: Dialing a pod’s IP on 8080 also gets you there, but it skips the extension: no random draw and no guarantee that pod still exists.

alternativas.texto: http://loja (port 80)
alternativas.explicacao: Right: the client uses the Service’s port (80, the http default), and the Service delivers to the targetPort (8080) of the drawn pod.

alternativas.texto: http://loja:8080
alternativas.explicacao: The Service doesn’t listen on 8080: that’s the port inside the pod. On the extension, the port is 80.

alternativas.texto: Both: the Service listens on both ports.
alternativas.explicacao: No: the Service only listens on the ports in its ports list (here, 80).

n3-quiz-ingress-sem-controlador.titulo: Quiz: the front desk with no staff
n3-quiz-ingress-sem-controlador.enunciado: In a cluster with no Ingress controller at all, you apply an Ingress that sends /api to the loja Service. What happens?
n3-quiz-ingress-sem-controlador.vidaReal: Hanging an “information desk” sign at a front gate with no staff: the sign is there, but nobody answers.
n3-quiz-ingress-sem-controlador.limite: At a real front gate, someone would find the unstaffed sign odd. Kubernetes doesn’t: the Ingress just sits there, with no ADDRESS, and nobody warns you.

alternativas.texto: The apply is rejected: the controller is missing.
alternativas.explicacao: The doorman accepts it: the Ingress is just an object kept in the book. He doesn’t check whether anyone will carry it out.

alternativas.texto: Kubernetes installs a controller on its own.
alternativas.explicacao: It doesn’t: picking and installing the controller (Traefik, NGINX, HAProxy...) is up to whoever runs the cluster.

alternativas.texto: The loja Service becomes a LoadBalancer.
alternativas.explicacao: The Ingress doesn’t change the Service: it just points to it.

alternativas.texto: The Ingress is created, but nothing starts answering.
alternativas.explicacao: Right: with no controller, nobody reads the rules. The Ingress has no address (the ADDRESS column is empty).

n4-quiz-aviso-mudou.titulo: Quiz: who sees the new notice?
n4-quiz-aviso-mudou.enunciado: Three pods read the loja-config ConfigMap, each in a different way. You change the ConfigMap. Which one sees the new value without restarting?
n4-quiz-aviso-mudou.vidaReal: Whoever has the poster hanging in the living room sees the new notice; whoever copied the notice into a notebook when moving in still has the old copy.
n4-quiz-aviso-mudou.limite: The poster changes by itself, but someone has to look again: a program that only reads the file when it starts won’t notice the change either.

alternativas.texto: The one that reads one key with env and configMapKeyRef.
alternativas.explicacao: The environment variable is read when the container is born and never changes again.

alternativas.texto: The one that reads all the keys with envFrom.
alternativas.explicacao: Those are environment variables too: they keep the value from birth.

alternativas.texto: The one that mounts the ConfigMap as a volume in a folder.
alternativas.explicacao: Right: the mounted file follows along by itself, within a minute or so. The exception: mounted with subPath (a single file, inside a folder that already exists), it doesn’t follow.

alternativas.texto: None: the kubelet restarts every pod when the ConfigMap changes.
alternativas.explicacao: Nobody restarts anything on their own. For the variables to change, you’re the one who runs kubectl rollout restart.

n4-quiz-mesa.titulo: Quiz: the desk after the fall
n4-quiz-mesa.enunciado: The nginx container in the placa pod crashed and the kubelet restarted it. What happened to what was in the emptyDir?
n4-quiz-mesa.vidaReal: The resident fainted and came to: the desk still has the papers on it. On a move (a new pod), the desk stays behind.
n4-quiz-mesa.limite: A real desk could go along on the move; the emptyDir never does: new pod, empty desk.

alternativas.texto: It vanished along with the container.
alternativas.explicacao: What vanishes on a restart is what was written to the container’s own disk, outside the volumes. The emptyDir belongs to the pod.

alternativas.texto: It’s still there: the pod is the same, and the emptyDir belongs to it.
alternativas.explicacao: Right: the emptyDir survives a container restart. It only vanishes when the pod goes away (deleted, evicted or replaced by a Deployment).

alternativas.texto: It was copied to a PVC.
alternativas.explicacao: Nobody copies anything to a PVC on their own: the PVC is a separate request of yours.

n4-quiz-volta-da-temporada.enunciado: You scaled db down from 3 replicas to 1, and the dados-db-1 and dados-db-2 PVCs stayed. Now you go back to 3. What does the new db-1 get?
n4-quiz-volta-da-temporada.vidaReal: The resident of number 1 comes back from a trip and storage unit 1 is right there, with their things inside.
n4-quiz-volta-da-temporada.limite: In the condo, nobody forgets a full storage unit. In the cluster, an idle PVC doesn’t warn anyone. You can ask for it to be deleted on scale-down (persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy), but then the data goes with it.

alternativas.texto: A new, empty disk.
alternativas.explicacao: The dados-db-1 PVC still exists: the StatefulSet doesn’t request another one.

alternativas.texto: A copy of db-0’s data.
alternativas.explicacao: The StatefulSet doesn’t copy data between replicas: that’s the program’s job (redis, postgres).

alternativas.texto: Nothing: db-1 won’t come back until someone deletes the old PVC.
alternativas.explicacao: The old PVC doesn’t get in the way: it’s exactly what db-1 is looking for.

alternativas.texto: The same dados-db-1 PVC, with the data from before.
alternativas.explicacao: Right: the PVC’s name follows the pod’s, and db-1 finds its storage unit again. That’s why the PVCs stay when the StatefulSet scales down.

n5-quiz-coleta-atrasada.enunciado: The limpeza (cleanup) job runs every 5 minutes. Today, one run took 7 minutes. What happens when the next one is due?
n5-quiz-coleta-atrasada.vidaReal: The 7:05 truck leaves even if the 7:00 one is still out: two trucks on the same block.
n5-quiz-coleta-atrasada.limite: Two trucks at once just snarl traffic; two Jobs at once can corrupt data (two backups writing the same file). For those, Forbid.

alternativas.texto: The CronJob waits for the late run to finish and only then starts the next one.
alternativas.explicacao: It never waits. With concurrencyPolicy: Forbid, it skips the new run.

alternativas.texto: Another run starts, at the same time as the late one.
alternativas.explicacao: Right: the default (concurrencyPolicy: Allow) lets both run together. Forbid skips the new one; Replace stops the old one and starts the new one.

alternativas.texto: The late run is canceled.
alternativas.explicacao: Only with concurrencyPolicy: Replace. The default leaves both running.

n5-quiz-fuso.enunciado: The backup CronJob has schedule: "0 3 * * *", with no timeZone. Conceição (the controller manager) keeps her clock on UTC, and the company runs on Brasília time (UTC−3). At what time, Brasília time, does the backup run?
n5-quiz-fuso.vidaReal: The pickup follows the management office’s clock, not yours: if the office sets its clock by Greenwich, its 3 a.m. is midnight in Brasília.
n5-quiz-fuso.limite: In the condo, everyone lives in the same time zone. A cloud cluster almost always uses UTC, wherever it is.

alternativas.texto: At 3 a.m.
alternativas.explicacao: That would be the case if the controller manager used Brasília time. It uses UTC.

alternativas.texto: At 6 a.m.
alternativas.explicacao: The math goes the other way: Brasília is 3 hours behind UTC, not ahead.

alternativas.texto: It depends on the time zone of the computer of whoever applied the YAML.
alternativas.explicacao: kubectl doesn’t send any time zone: the schedule is read by the controller manager, in the cluster.

alternativas.texto: At midnight.
alternativas.explicacao: Right: without spec.timeZone, the controller manager’s time zone applies (almost always UTC), and 3 a.m. UTC is midnight in Brasília. For 3 a.m. local time: timeZone: America/Sao_Paulo.

n6-quiz-readiness.enunciado: A loja pod was ready. Now its readinessProbe fails 3 times in a row, while the livenessProbe keeps passing. What happens?
n6-quiz-readiness.vidaReal: The clerk says “I can’t right now”: the front gate stops sending customers, but nobody pulls them out of the chair.
n6-quiz-readiness.limite: If everyone says “I can’t right now” at the same time, the extension has no one and the call is refused: readiness doesn’t call for backup.

alternativas.texto: The kubelet restarts the container.
alternativas.explicacao: Restarting is liveness’s job, and it’s passing. Readiness only decides whether the pod gets customers.

alternativas.texto: The Deployment deletes the pod and creates another.
alternativas.explicacao: Nobody deletes the pod because of readiness: it stays there, waiting to get better.

alternativas.texto: The pod leaves the Service’s endpoints (READY 0/1), but keeps running, and comes back when the probe passes.
alternativas.explicacao: Right: off the extension, no restart. When the probe passes again, the pod gets customers again.

alternativas.texto: Nothing changes: the pod is just marked as not ready.
alternativas.explicacao: It does change: a pod that isn’t ready stops getting customers through the Service.

n6-quiz-request-limit.titulo: Quiz: does the scheduler look at the limit?
n6-quiz-request-limit.enunciado: node-1 has 1 CPU left (adding up the requests of everyone already living there). A pod arrives with requests.cpu: 500m and limits.cpu: 2. Can the scheduler put it on node-1?
n6-quiz-request-limit.vidaReal: The building accepts a resident based on their contracted power; their circuit breaker can be bigger than what the building has left, because not everyone turns everything on at once.
n6-quiz-request-limit.limite: If everyone draws up to their limit at the same time, CPU gets shared (everyone slows down); memory can’t be shared: someone gets killed or evicted.

alternativas.texto: No: a 2-CPU limit doesn’t fit in 1.
alternativas.explicacao: The scheduler doesn’t look at the limit, only the request. The limit can go beyond what the node has.

alternativas.texto: Only if the pod is using less than 1 CPU right now.
alternativas.explicacao: The scheduler doesn’t look at usage (kubectl top): the pod hasn’t even started. It adds up the reservations.

alternativas.texto: Yes: the scheduler only adds up requests; the limit is the usage ceiling.
alternativas.explicacao: Right: 500m fits in the 1 CPU left. The limit of 2 only says how far the container can draw, if there’s free CPU.

n6-quiz-hpa-replicas.titulo: Quiz: the manager and the file
n6-quiz-hpa-replicas.enunciado: The HPA took loja to 6 replicas. In the middle of the sale, someone applies loja.yaml, which says replicas: 2. What happens?
n6-quiz-hpa-replicas.vidaReal: The manager hired 6 temps; the old contract arrives saying 2 and HR lets 4 go. Minutes later, the manager hires again.
n6-quiz-hpa-replicas.limite: In a real HR department, someone would notice the tug-of-war. In the cluster nobody warns you: the number goes up and down, and customers feel it.

alternativas.texto: The store drops to 2, and the HPA scales back up on its next calculation: the two fight.
alternativas.explicacao: Right. With an HPA, leave replicas out of the YAML: the manager decides the number.

alternativas.texto: The apply is rejected, because the HPA is in charge of the replicas.
alternativas.explicacao: apply doesn’t know about the HPA: it writes what the file says.

alternativas.texto: The HPA locks the number at 6, and the apply ignores the field.
alternativas.explicacao: The HPA doesn’t lock anything: it just changes replicas from time to time, like anyone else.

alternativas.texto: The HPA is deleted.
alternativas.explicacao: No: the HPA is a separate object and stays there (hence the fight).

n7-quiz-toleration.titulo: Quiz: does the authorization take you there?
n7-quiz-toleration.enunciado: node-2 has the taint dedicado=gpu:NoSchedule. A pod has the toleration for that taint and no nodeSelector or affinity. Where can it land?
n7-quiz-toleration.vidaReal: Authorization to enter the GPU building isn’t an order to move there: the authorized resident may very well live in a regular building.
n7-quiz-toleration.limite: In the condo, whoever has authorization usually goes to the special building. In the cluster, the real-estate agent ignores the authorization when choosing: only the nodeSelector (or affinity) pulls the pod there.

alternativas.texto: Only on node-2.
alternativas.explicacao: The toleration doesn’t take anyone there: it just moves the sign out of the way.

alternativas.texto: On node-1 or node-2: the toleration allows node-2, it doesn’t force it.
alternativas.explicacao: Right. To go only to node-2, combine the toleration with a nodeSelector (dedicado: gpu).

alternativas.texto: Nowhere: it stays Pending.
alternativas.explicacao: node-1 has no taint at all: any pod gets in.

alternativas.texto: On any node, including the control-plane.
alternativas.explicacao: The control-plane has a different taint (node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane), which this toleration doesn’t cover.

n7-quiz-uncordon.enunciado: You emptied node-1 (kubectl drain), swapped the disk and ran kubectl uncordon node-1. What happens to the pods that left it?
n7-quiz-uncordon.vidaReal: The renovation is over and the building reopened, but nobody moves back just because the sign came down.
n7-quiz-uncordon.limite: Real residents might want to go back. In the cluster, the node stays empty until new pods arrive (a rollout, one more replica).

alternativas.texto: They go back to node-1 on their own.
alternativas.explicacao: Nobody tells them to go back: uncordon only lifts the closure.

alternativas.texto: The scheduler redistributes everything, to balance the nodes.
alternativas.explicacao: The scheduler only chooses on arrival: it never moves a pod that’s already running.

alternativas.texto: They stay where they are; only the next pods can go to node-1.
alternativas.explicacao: Right: the node accepts new pods again, and the old ones stay on the other nodes until they’re replaced.

n7-quiz-pdb.titulo: Quiz: what does the PDB hold back?
n7-quiz-pdb.enunciado: loja has 3 replicas and a PDB with minAvailable: 2. Which of these situations does the PDB hold back?
n7-quiz-pdb.vidaReal: The elevator agreement holds for the scheduled renovation; if the power goes out, the building goes down with whoever is inside.
n7-quiz-pdb.limite: In the condo, breaking the agreement starts a fight. In the cluster, a kubectl delete runs right over the PDB without even asking.

alternativas.texto: node-1 loses power, with 2 of the store’s pods inside.
alternativas.explicacao: An outage doesn’t ask permission: the PDB has nobody to say “no” to.

alternativas.texto: A kubectl delete pod on all 3 pods.
alternativas.explicacao: delete doesn’t go through the eviction API: the PDB isn’t even consulted.

alternativas.texto: A version change of the store (the rolling update).
alternativas.explicacao: The version change follows the Deployment’s maxUnavailable, not the PDB.

alternativas.texto: A kubectl drain that would leave only 1 pod ready.
alternativas.explicacao: Right: drain evicts through the eviction API, which checks the PDB and waits for the replacements to be ready.

n8-quiz-rolebinding.titulo: Quiz: how far does the badge reach?
n8-quiz-rolebinding.enunciado: A RoleBinding in the loja namespace gives ana the view ClusterRole. Where can Ana read?
n8-quiz-rolebinding.vidaReal: The “visitor” badge design belongs to the whole condo, but block B’s front desk only hands out badges that open block B.
n8-quiz-rolebinding.limite: A real badge can be lent. In the cluster, it’s valid only for whoever received it (User, Group or ServiceAccount).

alternativas.texto: In every namespace, because view is a ClusterRole.
alternativas.explicacao: The reach is decided by the handout, not the badge: a RoleBinding only counts in its own namespace.

alternativas.texto: Only in the loja namespace.
alternativas.explicacao: Right. The ClusterRole is just the badge design. To count in every namespace, it’s a ClusterRoleBinding.

alternativas.texto: Nowhere: a RoleBinding can’t point to a ClusterRole.
alternativas.explicacao: It can, and it’s common: that’s how view, edit and admin get reused across namespaces, without copying the Role.

n8-quiz-cni.enunciado: You apply a NetworkPolicy that closes ingress to every pod in the namespace. It’s accepted, but everything still gets through. What could be the reason?
n8-quiz-cni.vidaReal: The management office approved the turnstile on paper, but nobody installed it at the door: the paper is on file, and the door is still open.
n8-quiz-cni.limite: On a real building site, someone would see the door with no turnstile. In the cluster, the policy shows up in kubectl get netpol as if it worked.

alternativas.texto: The policy only applies to pods created after it.
alternativas.explicacao: It applies right away, to pods that already exist too.

alternativas.texto: NetworkPolicy only blocks what comes from other namespaces.
alternativas.explicacao: It blocks from anywhere, including the same namespace.

alternativas.texto: The cluster’s network plugin (CNI) doesn’t implement NetworkPolicy.
alternativas.explicacao: Right: the API stores the policy, but the CNI is what blocks the packets. With one that doesn’t implement it, the policy is just decoration, with no error at all.

n8-quiz-catracas-somam.titulo: Quiz: two turnstiles on the same door
n8-quiz-catracas-somam.enunciado: In the rede namespace, two policies select the api: nega-tudo (deny-all, closes ingress) and the one that allows ingress from app=vitrine. Does the storefront get through?
n8-quiz-catracas-somam.vidaReal: Each new turnstile is one more list of who may pass: the doorman lets in anyone on any of the lists.
n8-quiz-catracas-somam.limite: In a building, a “no entry” sign can outweigh a pass. Here there’s no “no entry” sign: what closes the door is the lack of a pass.

alternativas.texto: No: deny beats allow.
alternativas.explicacao: A NetworkPolicy has no way to deny: each one only allows, and the allowances add up.

alternativas.texto: It depends on which policy was applied last.
alternativas.explicacao: Order doesn’t matter: there’s no priority between them.

alternativas.texto: Yes: the rules add up, and whatever any of them allows gets through.
alternativas.explicacao: Right. nega-tudo only “closes” because it selects the pods without allowing anything; the other one adds an allowance.

n9-quiz-previous.enunciado: The database crashes every minute (RESTARTS keeps climbing). Right now it’s Running again, and kubectl logs NAME only shows the startup, with no error at all. Where is the error message?
n9-quiz-previous.vidaReal: The resident faints, is woken up and remembers nothing: what they said before fainting is in yesterday’s journal.
n9-quiz-previous.limite: The cluster only keeps the previous attempt: older ones are lost. To keep everything, logs are shipped somewhere else (Loki, Elasticsearch).

alternativas.texto: In kubectl logs NAME --previous.
alternativas.explicacao: Right: the container running now is a different one, which just started. The error stayed in the previous attempt’s log.

alternativas.texto: Nowhere: the log vanishes along with the container that crashed.
alternativas.explicacao: The kubelet keeps the last attempt’s log: that’s what --previous shows.

alternativas.texto: In kubectl get pods -o wide.
alternativas.explicacao: That shows the node and the IP, not what the program wrote.

n9-quiz-apagar-o-pod.titulo: Quiz: does deleting the pod fix it?
n9-quiz-apagar-o-pod.enunciado: The vitrine (storefront) pods, from a Deployment, are in ImagePullBackOff: the YAML asks for nginx:1.27-vitrine, a tag that was never pushed to the registry. You delete one of them with kubectl delete pod. What happens?
n9-quiz-apagar-o-pod.vidaReal: Throwing out the defective prefab module doesn’t help if the factory order still has the wrong model: another identical one arrives.
n9-quiz-apagar-o-pod.limite: Sometimes deleting the pod does fix it: when the defect was in the pod (a stuck state, a bad node), not in the blueprint.

alternativas.texto: Another pod is born, and this time the image is found.
alternativas.explicacao: The new pod comes from the same template, which still asks for the tag that doesn’t exist in the registry.

alternativas.texto: The storefront is left with one pod fewer.
alternativas.explicacao: The Deployment (through the ReplicaSet) replaces the pod right away.

alternativas.texto: Another pod is born, with the same wrong image, and the error comes back.
alternativas.explicacao: Right: the fix goes in the Deployment (in the YAML or with kubectl set image). Then the pods are replaced on their own.

n10-quiz-install-de-novo.enunciado: The loja release is already installed. To change the version, someone runs helm install loja kube-learn/loja --set image.tag=1.1. What happens?
n10-quiz-install-de-novo.vidaReal: Asking the builder for a new build with the name of one that already exists: they refuse and tell you to request a renovation.
n10-quiz-install-de-novo.limite: Two builds with the same name can exist, in different blocks: a release name is unique only within its namespace.

alternativas.texto: The loja release is updated to 1.1.
alternativas.explicacao: That’s helm upgrade. install only creates a new release.

alternativas.texto: Error: the name loja is already in use, and nothing changes.
alternativas.explicacao: Right. To change an existing release: helm upgrade (or helm upgrade --install, which installs it if it doesn’t exist yet).

alternativas.texto: A second loja is born, next to the first.
alternativas.explicacao: In the same namespace, the release name is unique. For a second one, use another name.

alternativas.texto: The release is deleted and installed again.
alternativas.explicacao: Helm doesn’t delete anything without a helm uninstall.

n10-quiz-overlay.titulo: Quiz: does the overlay touch the base?
n10-quiz-overlay.enunciado: overlays/prod asks for 3 replicas and tag 1.1. You run kubectl apply -k overlays/prod. What happens to base/deployment.yaml?
n10-quiz-overlay.vidaReal: The branch’s sheet says “here, 3 clerks”: the original blueprint stays in the drawer, unchanged, for the other cities.
n10-quiz-overlay.limite: A paper sheet gets filed away; Kustomize’s output isn’t kept anywhere. To see what went to the cluster, run kubectl kustomize again.

alternativas.texto: It’s rewritten with replicas: 3 and tag 1.1.
alternativas.explicacao: Kustomize never writes to your files: it only reads them.

alternativas.texto: Nothing: Kustomize builds the result on the fly, and only the result goes to the cluster.
alternativas.explicacao: Right. The base stays the same, and the other overlays (dev, staging) keep building on it.

alternativas.texto: It stays the same, but the dev overlay gets 3 replicas too.
alternativas.explicacao: Each overlay only sees the base and its own tweaks: dev doesn’t even know prod exists.

n10-quiz-crd-sem-operador.titulo: Quiz: the form with no specialist
n10-quiz-crd-sem-operador.enunciado: In a cluster with the backups.kube-learn.dev CRD, but without the backup operator, you apply the noturno (nightly) Backup. What happens?
n10-quiz-crd-sem-operador.vidaReal: The backup request is accepted at the front desk and filed, but the specialist hasn’t been hired yet: the request sits in the pile.
n10-quiz-crd-sem-operador.limite: When the specialist arrives, they read the whole pile: the operator also handles the requests that already existed.

alternativas.texto: The apply is rejected: the operator is missing.
alternativas.explicacao: The CRD has already taught the API the new kind: the Backup is accepted (and validated against the schema).

alternativas.texto: Kubernetes creates the backup’s CronJob on its own.
alternativas.explicacao: Kubernetes doesn’t know what a Backup means: the operator is the one that creates the CronJob.

alternativas.texto: The Backup is stored (kubectl get backups shows it), but no backup is made.
alternativas.explicacao: Right: the CRD only stores the request. The operator is the one that acts.

n11-quiz-pdb-rollout.titulo: Quiz: who holds the line during a version change?
n11-quiz-pdb-rollout.enunciado: loja has 4 replicas, a PDB with minAvailable: 3 and a rolling update with maxUnavailable: 0. During the version change, what guarantees the ready pods?
n11-quiz-pdb-rollout.vidaReal: The elevator agreement is with the management office, for building maintenance; the store’s renovation follows the store’s own rules.
n11-quiz-pdb-rollout.limite: In real life, an “at least 3” agreement would cover everything. In the cluster, each rule only counts for whoever checks it.

alternativas.texto: The PDB.
alternativas.explicacao: The PDB only applies to evictions through the eviction API (drain). The rollout doesn’t even check the PDB.

alternativas.texto: Both together: the stricter one wins.
alternativas.explicacao: They don’t combine: the rollout doesn’t check the PDB, and drain doesn’t look at the strategy.

alternativas.texto: The Deployment’s strategy (maxUnavailable: 0).
alternativas.explicacao: Right. Each one protects a different moment: the strategy, the version change; the PDB, node maintenance.

n11-quiz-normas-e-pods-antigos.titulo: Quiz: the new code and the current residents
n11-quiz-normas-e-pods-antigos.enunciado: The legado namespace has pods running as root. You give it the label pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted. What happens to those pods?
n11-quiz-normas-e-pods-antigos.vidaReal: The fire marshals’ new code applies to whoever moves in from now on; whoever already lives there stays, until they leave.
n11-quiz-normas-e-pods-antigos.limite: Real fire marshals could condemn a noncompliant apartment. Pod Security can’t: it only stops people at the door.

alternativas.texto: They’re evicted on the spot.
alternativas.explicacao: The fire marshals don’t evict anyone: the code applies when pods are created.

alternativas.texto: kubectl label is rejected while any pod breaks the code.
alternativas.explicacao: The label is accepted; the response just comes with a warning.

alternativas.texto: They keep running: kubectl label only warns (Warning) which ones break the code.
alternativas.explicacao: Right. Careful: if one of them crashes or gets replaced, the new pod is rejected. Fix the pods before setting the code.

alternativas.texto: They’re restarted as a regular user.
alternativas.explicacao: Pod Security doesn’t change pods: it only accepts or rejects them.
